planting.note: Plant container stock in spring in well-drained soil in full sun against a strong, permanent structure; Morning Calm is a J.C. Raulston Arboretum introduction of Chinese trumpet vine with a slower, more woody, better-behaved habit than the straight species.

directions: Morning Calm is a J.C. Raulston Arboretum introduction of Chinese trumpet vine selected for enormous, open-faced apricot-orange flowers with yellow throats that appear in flushes through summer and draw hummingbirds from a distance. Compared with straight-species Chinese trumpet vine, it grows in a slower, more woody, better-behaved habit, making it easier to keep within bounds on a large arbor or pergola than the rampant American trumpet creeper. Provide a sturdy, permanent support in full sun, since the vine's woody framework becomes substantial with age; once established it tolerates heat and drought well. Prune hard in late winter to control size and to encourage the current season's flowering wood.

common_name: Chinese Evergreen Climbing Hydrangea Vine (Round-Leaved Hydrangea Vine)

planting.note: Root semi-hardwood cuttings in summer, or plant container-grown vines in spring against a sheltered wall or tree trunk in moist, humus-rich soil; Decumaria sinensis is less cold-hardy than the American climbing hydrangea vine and needs winter protection outside zones 8-9.

directions: Decumaria sinensis is the evergreen Chinese counterpart to the native American climbing hydrangea vine (D. barbara), climbing by self-clinging aerial roots without need for tying or a trellis. In late spring it produces honey-scented sprays of small creamy-yellow flowers set against narrow, glossy, dark-green evergreen foliage that persists year-round in favorable sites. It is noticeably less vigorous and less cold-hardy than its American relative, so give it a sheltered position such as a south- or west-facing wall or a tree trunk out of harsh winter wind, especially near the northern edge of its range. Grow in consistently moist, humus-rich, well-drained soil in full sun to partial shade; established vines tolerate brief cold snaps but appreciate a protective mulch over the root zone going into winter.

planting.note: Plant container vines in spring in average, well-drained soil in full sun to part shade against a trellis, arbor, or fence, since Akebia twines and does not self-cling; Rosea is the pink-flowered form of chocolate vine, similar in vigor to the species.

directions: Rosea is the pink-flowered selection of five-leaf akebia, producing dangling spring clusters of rich mauve-pink, waxy flowers with an intoxicating chocolate-and-vanilla fragrance held above dark green, five-parted palmate leaflets. Like the species, it twines rather than clings, so give it a trellis, arbor, or wire support to climb, and expect vigorous growth that needs an annual post-bloom pruning to stay in bounds. Cross-pollination with another Akebia cultivar or the species improves fruit set, yielding unusual sausage-shaped purple pods with sweet, edible white pulp in fall. Semi-evergreen in mild winters and fully deciduous farther north, it tolerates a wide range of soils and light levels from full sun to fairly deep shade.

planting.note: Plant container vines after all danger of frost has passed in well-drained, moderately fertile soil in full sun to light shade; in zones below 9, grow in a large container and move indoors or to a bright greenhouse before the first frost.

directions: Golden passionflower produces small, star-shaped, citrus-yellow flowers that appear in flushes nearly year-round in frost-free climates, drawing hummingbirds and bees to the garden. Unlike many tropical passionflowers, it tolerates a range of light from full sun to fairly bright shade and stays comparatively compact and easy to manage on a small trellis, obelisk, or large container. It roots readily from cuttings and is self-fertile, so a single plant reliably sets its small, elongated yellow fruits without needing a second vine nearby. In climates colder than zone 9 it has little cold tolerance, so grow it in a container and bring it into a bright, frost-free location for winter.
